title: The Scholars
subtitle: Fame and Fortune Have No Foundation · All Efforts of the Heart Come to Nothing
description: The Scholars is a full-length satirical novel by the Qing-dynasty writer Wu Jingzi, comprising fifty-six chapters. It is the pinnacle of classical Chinese satirical literature. Set against the backdrop of the Ming dynasty, the novel unfolds through a series of relatively independent yet interconnected stories, exposing the corrosive effect of the imperial examination system on the souls of scholars — Fan Jin going mad upon passing the provincial exam, Yan Jiansheng picking at his lamp wick on his deathbed, Kuang Chaoren's moral degeneration and ingratitude. Each image is a mirror of satire, reflecting the collective predicament of the literati in the twilight of the feudal age.

route.title: The Scholars: Fame and Glory Are but a Dream — How Few Remain Clear-Eyed
route.intro:
Some resign office and return to their hometown; others race through the night to the examination hall. In youth one knows no taste of sorrow; only in old age does one understand how hard the road has been.
Wu Jingzi (1701–1754), style name Minxuan, literary name Limin, was a native of Quanjiao in Anhui. He came from a family of scholars who had passed the imperial examinations over several generations, yet he himself repeatedly failed. In middle age he moved to Nanjing, settling by the Qinhuai River, making a living by selling his writing, living in poverty and obscurity. It was this experience of destitution that allowed him to see through the absurd nature of the examination system. He transformed his own suffering and insight into The Scholars, using acrid satire and deep compassion to leave behind the clear-eyed monologue of an age where "all pursuits are base, only scholarship is exalted." Let us enter the Jiangnan world of The Scholars — from the Jiangnan Examination Hall in Nanjing to the He Garden in Yangzhou, from the Yue Fei Temple in Hangzhou to the waterways of Shaoxing — visiting the national heritage sites that bear witness to the rise and fall of the examination system and the souls of the scholar-literati.

stops.title: Stop One: Nanjing · The Many Faces of the Jiangnan Examination Hall
stops.content: Chapter Three of The Scholars, "Fan Jin Passes the Provincial Exam," contains the most classic satirical passage in Chinese literary history. Fan Jin, a fifty-four-year-old lifelong candidate whose family was so poor the pot could not even boil, suddenly passes the provincial exam. When the good news arrives, he cries out — "Yi! Wonderful! I passed!" — and before the words are out, he has gone mad. After being slapped back to his senses by the butcher his father-in-law, Fan Jin transforms from a poverty-stricken scholar no one respected into a successful candidate everyone curries favor with. The magic of the examination system is laid bare in this absurd scene. The Chaotian Palace near the Confucius Temple in Nanjing was an important Ming-Qing landmark, while the Zhan Garden on the banks of the Qinhuai River — the Ming-dynasty residence of Xu Da, Prince Zhongshan — bore witness to the joys and sorrows of countless scholars emerging from the examination hall. Every time the provincial exam results were announced, the taverns and teahouses on both sides of the Qinhuai River were packed with ecstatic successful candidates and dispirited failures. Wu Jingzi lived by this very Qinhuai River, watching the joys and sorrows of these scholars day after day. His portrayal of Fan Jin was also a bitter laugh at his own expense. The Chaotian Palace is itself an architectural history. Known as the "foremost historic site of Jinling," it was first built in the Ming Hongwu reign, originally called "Hongwu Palace," where civil and military officials rehearsed court ceremonial rites. The existing buildings date from the Tongzhi reign of the Qing dynasty: the Lingxing Gate, Dacheng Gate, Dacheng Hall, and Chongsheng Hall ascend in sequence along the central axis, their yellow glazed tiles gleaming in the sunlight. The four characters "万仞宫墙" (Ten-Thousand-Ren Palace Wall) are set into the red screen wall, each character about a meter square, solemn and majestic. When Wu Jingzi passed by here, how starkly the officials rehearsing court rites contrasted with the scholars laboring in the examination hall — on one side, the glory of success; on the other, the humiliation of failure. The Zhan Garden offers a different flavor. This Ming-dynasty princely garden, covering over 20,000 square meters, is famous for its rockeries — the Taihu limestone of the "Southern Rockery" forms layered peaks and deep caves, making you feel as if you were deep in the mountains. When Wu Jingzi wrote Ma Chunshang (Mr. Ma the Second) visiting West Lake — "gazing at the row of taverns along the lake, each hanging plump legs of mutton..." — the poverty and longing of the destitute scholar facing a world of plenty make a jarring contrast with the exquisitely refined life in the Zhan Garden. The greatness of The Scholars lies in Wu Jingzi's ability to see through the illusion of fame and fortune while feeling deep sympathy for those ordinary people devoured by the examination system. His satire was not aimed at Fan Jin, but at the age that drove people mad.

stops.title: Stop Two: Nanjing · Lamenting Rise and Fall Before the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum
stops.content: Wu Jingzi lived in Nanjing for nearly twenty years. His impoverished years by the Qinhuai River gave him intimate knowledge of every corner of the city. Many of the stories in The Scholars are set in Nanjing — gatherings of notable personages, literary soirees, meetings of talented scholars — but behind all this refinement lies a desolate world-weariness. The spirit-way of the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum winds long and sinuous, the stone statues standing silent for six hundred years. Wu Jingzi must also have walked this spirit-way. At the end of his novel he writes: "The misty clouds of Jiangzuo, the old worthies of Huainan — written into a broken text, it all breaks the heart." Is not fame itself just a dream? Whether you pass the exam or not, in the end it is all just a handful of yellow earth. And the Nanjing City Wall — the longest ancient city wall in the world — has seen so many scholars come and go, rise and fall. The wall still stands as imposing as ever, but those who hurried to the examinations have long scattered into the dust of history. The architectural details of the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum are full of hidden meaning. The spirit-way is not a traditional straight line but winds in curves — it is said to have been designed to avoid Plum Blossom Hill, where Sun Quan's tomb lies. Flanking the spirit-way are twelve pairs of six kinds of stone beasts — lions, xiezhi, camels, elephants, qilins, and horses — two standing and two crouching, standing silent guard for over six hundred years. The stone attendants, four civil officials holding tablets and four military officers in armor and swords, stand with solemn dignity. These stones have warmth — glistening with a blue sheen in the rain, radiating warmth in the sun. For six hundred years, countless scholars have passed them, some triumphant, some heartbroken. The stones have seen it all and say nothing. And the Nanjing City Wall — the world's longest ancient city wall at thirty-five kilometers — its most moving feature is not its grandeur but the inscriptions on its bricks. Every brick bears the name of the maker, the place of origin, the date of firing. Wu Jingzi may have traced these inscriptions with his fingers. The names of these anonymous craftsmen, carved into the bricks, have endured for six hundred years — while the names of countless top-scoring graduates are already forgotten. That is perhaps a profound form of satire: true dignity lies not on the honor roll of the examination hall, but in the actual bricks and tiles of the real world.

stops.title: Stop Three: Yangzhou · The Pristine Stream Hidden Deep in He Garden
stops.content: In The Scholars, Du Shaoqing is Wu Jingzi's self-portrait — he spent money like water to make friends with famous scholars, preferring poverty to bowing before the powerful. The prototype for this figure partly came from the literary circle of Yangzhou. In the Qing dynasty, Yangzhou was a gathering place for salt merchants and a cultural high ground of Jiangnan. Those "marketplace eccentrics" who refused to take official positions — calligraphers, painters, musicians, chess players — became the warmest characters in Wu Jingzi's novel. The He Garden was built by He Zhidao in the Qing Guangxu reign after he resigned from office and retired. The innovation of this garden lies in its extensive use of Western elements. The double-storied covered corridor, fifteen hundred meters long, earned it the title "foremost garden of the late Qing." The Pianshi Shanfang within the garden is said to be the only surviving rockery masterpiece by the monk-painter Shi Tao. The garden's owner had also seen through the darkness of officialdom and chosen to retreat — how similar to the state of mind of the disenchanted scholars in Wu Jingzi's novel. Fame and fortune are but fleeting clouds; a garden and a few volumes of poetry are the true dwelling places of the soul. Entering the He Garden, one gets the full sense of why it is called the "foremost garden of the late Qing." The garden is divided into four parts: the Eastern Garden, the Western Garden, the residential area, and Pianshi Shanfang. The most stunning feature is the fifteen-hundred-meter double-storied covered corridor — two stories, the corridor waist winding sinuously, the eaves rising high like beak points. Walking through the corridor, you can scarcely tell whether it is sunny or raining. The latticed windows on the corridor walls borrow and reveal scenes — every window frame is a living painting. The stage is built over the water, carrying the idea of "moon in the water, flowers in the mirror" to its extreme. When actors perform Kunqu opera on the stage, the ripples of the water carry the sound, and sitting in the corridor on the opposite bank, the music sounds as if from another world. In The Scholars, Wu Jingzi created the character Du Shaoqing — a scion of a wealthy family who squanders his fortune making friends with famous scholars, laughing uproariously even when he cannot afford a meal. Some scholars believe Du Shaoqing is Wu Jingzi's self-portrayal. Another unforgettable character is Ji Xianian — one of the "four eccentrics" — a poor calligrapher selling his writing on the street, who wrote beautifully but scorned the idea of writing New Year couplets for the rich to earn silver. These marketplace eccentrics, like He Zhidao who retired to his garden, each answered a question in their own way: when you are unwilling to drift along in this muddy world, how should you live?

stops.title: Stop Four: Hangzhou · Distinguishing Loyalty and Treachery Before Yue Fei's Temple
stops.content: A recurring theme in The Scholars is the idea of "true versus false scholars" — some talk endlessly of morality and literature while their hearts are filled with nothing but fame and profit; others appear down-and-out but possess hearts as open and upright as a whetstone. This interrogation of truth and falsehood takes on a particularly sharp edge before the Yue Fei Temple in Hangzhou. Before the Tomb of Yue Fei, the kneeling statues of Qin Hui and the other three traitors are forever fixed in eternal disgrace. Loyalty and treachery, good and evil — history is the ultimate judge. The screen wall, spirit-way, and gate-towers before the tomb are solemn and dignified, with stelae from successive dynasties lining both sides. Wu Jingzi's satire of hypocrites in The Scholars is like the contempt expressed for Qin Hui before Yue Fei's temple — time is the fairest arbiter; gold and silver cannot be taken away, but deeds and faults are judged by posterity. Looking up from the foot of Qixia Ridge, Yue Fei's "utmost loyalty in serving the state" forms a glaring contrast with the scheming, self-serving characters in Wu Jingzi's novel. The architectural layout of the Tomb of Yue Fei was formed through over eight hundred years of repairs. Three pairs of stone attendants and three pairs of stone animals — horses, sheep, and tigers — line the spirit-way in front of the tomb, all Ming-dynasty reconstructions. The stone sheep are gentle, the stone tigers ferocious, the stone figures solemn. The tomb gate faces west — a deliberate choice: after Yue Fei was wrongfully killed, people wanted his soul to gaze forever toward the lost northern homeland. The four characters "尽忠报国" (Utmost Loyalty in Serving the State) on the screen wall are said to be written by Yue Fei himself — bold strokes, the force of a thousand years penetrating through. There is one particularly satirical passage in The Scholars. After Fan Jin passes the provincial exam, his father-in-law Hu the butcher's attitude toward him changes in an instant: "I've always said, this worthy son-in-law of mine is both learned and handsome..." The moment before, he had called Fan Jin a "pointy-faced monkey"; the next moment, he praises his "good looks." Wu Jingzi wrote this not to mock Hu the butcher — a market man who slaughters pigs — but to tell the reader: before the supremacy of fame and success, anyone can become a snob. Before the Yue Fei Temple, loyalty and treachery are clearly distinguished, but in the examination hall of The Scholars, the line between good and evil blurs — and that is the most profound tragedy of all.

stops.title: Stop Five: Suzhou and Shaoxing · The Scholar's Last Peach Blossom Spring
stops.content: The ending of The Scholars has no earth-shaking conclusion — the four eccentrics each make their living through their own craft: one writes calligraphy, one plays chess, one paints, one plays the zither. Wu Jingzi uses these four "marketplace eccentrics" to present his own answer: true dignity lies not in official rank but in the freedom to do what you love. The Humble Administrator's Garden in Suzhou — built by Wang Xianchen after he abandoned his official post and returned home — is a perfect expression of this spirit. And at the Shaoxing Ancient Bridge Group (including the Bazizi Bridge), black-canopied boats glide serenely beneath a Southern Song stone bridge — this living daily reality is more moving than any grand narrative. From Suzhou gardens to the Shaoxing water country, from the scholar's desk to the smoke and fire of the market — Wu Jingzi, through The Scholars, tells us that the true meaning of life lies not in the examination papers of the examination hall, but in the sound of flowing water beneath the bridge. The Humble Administrator's Garden is the supreme model of the literati garden. In the Ming Zhengde reign, Wang Xianchen was dismissed from office and returned to his hometown, giving the garden its name meaning "the humble one's way of governing," and inviting his friend Wen Zhengming to participate in the design. The entire garden takes water as its core; water covers three-fifths of the area. The pond is broad, the trees lush, the pavilions and terraces scattered in elegant disorder. The Fragrant Snow Pavilion has windows on all four sides; when the summer lotuses bloom, you feel as if you are amidst a sea of flowers. From the See-the-Hill Tower, you can borrow the distant North Temple Pagoda into the garden's scenery. The wisteria planted by Wen Zhengming's own hand still lives after over four hundred years, its gnarled vines like a coiling dragon, its blossoms cascading like a purple waterfall — Wu Jingzi surely saw this wisteria, for when he wrote about Suzhou in The Scholars, his tone was particularly gentle. The Shaoxing Ancient Bridge Group (including the Bazizi Bridge) is living heritage. The Bazizi Bridge, named for its two intersecting spans forming a "八" (eight) shape, was built in the Southern Song Jiatai reign. Beneath the bridge, black-canopied boats glide past, the old boatmen humming Shaoxing folk songs. At the end of his novel, Wu Jingzi wrote of four "marketplace eccentrics" — the calligrapher Ji Xianian, Wang Tai who sold firecrackers, Gai Kuan who ran a teahouse, and Jing Yuan the tailor. These most ordinary of craftsmen, each living a dignified and free life through their own skills, "neither coveting the wealth of the rich nor kowtowing to their moods." By then Wu Jingzi was already impoverished and destitute, but he wrote with calm equanimity — because those who have truly understood life do not worry.

stops.title: Stop Six: Quanjiao · Tracing the Homeland of The Scholars
stops.content:
Quanjiao in Anhui is Wu Jingzi's hometown. He was born into the Wu clan of Quanjiao — a family of scholars for five consecutive generations — yet he ultimately became the most profound critic of the system that had made his family. Along the Xiang River in Quanjiao, the memories of Wu Jingzi's youth are still preserved — the days reciting the Four Books and Five Classics in the private school, the nights listening to elders discuss their experiences in officialdom at family gatherings — all became the most vivid material of his later writing.

Wu Jingzi's former residence is located in Xianghe Township, Quanjiao County. It is a typical Huizhou-style building — three courtyards, white walls and black tiles, horse-head walls rising high. The Wu Jingzi Memorial Hall within displays his life in detail: from a scion of a family of scholars to a down-and-out literary man. At thirty-three, he sold off his family property in Quanjiao and moved with his wife to Nanjing — "the fields and houses all sold, the villagers spoke of him as a warning to their sons." This very act of "ruining the family" gave him true freedom — free from the burden of ancestral property, he also cast off the shackles of the examination system. Standing by the Qinhuai River, he could gaze at a world twisted by the pursuit of fame with a cool eye and a warm heart. This former residence in Quanjiao preserves forever the image of what he was before he set out.

From Quanjiao, traveling a short distance west brings you to the Drunken Old Man's Pavilion in Chuzhou — the birthplace of Ouyang Xiu's timeless essay: "The old drunkard's delight is not in wine, but in the mountains and waters." Wu Jingzi must have come here as a young man. The landscape of Chuzhou, the literary atmosphere of the Drunken Old Man's Pavilion, and the native soil of Quanjiao together nourished the soul of a great satirist. In The Scholars he wielded scathing satire against the examination system, but between the lines his writing is filled with profound compassion for the scholarly class — because he himself had walked that road. Standing before the gate of Wu Jingzi's former residence in Quanjiao, the bluestone-paved road stretches into the distance — the starting point of a young man's journey to Nanjing, to literature, to eternity.
